claims.text: The catalyst's high ethanol oxidation performance is governed by dynamic formation and reduction of a thin surface platinum oxide layer during operation.
The surface platinum oxide layer modifies adsorption energies of reaction intermediates.
Modified intermediate adsorption promotes multi-electron and multi-proton transfer and enhances catalyst durability.
The initial nanoscale platinum-group-metal catalyst has a pristine metallic surface without significant oxidation.
Electrochemical potential cycling can be controlled to promote or suppress dynamic surface platinum oxide formation.
Cyclic-voltammetric sweeps can traverse a platinum oxide formation region, whereas suitable potential holds can minimize oxide formation.
Transient surface oxidation occurs around specific potentials during potential cycling.
Surface oxidation alters the electronic structure of catalytic surface sites.
The oxidation-induced electronic change reduces the binding energy of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Reduced intermediate binding enhances ethanol activation and facilitates its 12-electron and 12-proton oxidation process.
Dynamic oxide formation reduces the buildup of poisoning intermediates.
Reduced poisoning improves catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
Activity and durability will be optimized at a controlled degree of reversibly formed platinum oxide.
Suppressing oxide formation will decrease catalytic performance because adsorption energies become suboptimal.
Sustained high potential and excessive oxide formation will decrease performance through suboptimal adsorption and/or irreversible oxidation.
The proposed mechanism applies in potential regimes permitting reversible oxide formation but may fail at potentials too low for oxide formation or high enough to cause irreversible oxidation.
Earlier reports on platinum-group metals and nanoscale catalysts support a role for surface oxidation dynamics.
